originalLocation.context: Posted by Zhongpu Consulting · AI Application Platform Advisory Dify has become one of our most-recommended platforms for clients who need a visual, low-code environment to build and iterate on LLM-powered applications. The combination of RAG pipelines, agent workflows, and an integrated evaluation framework in a single UI is genuinely compelling — it dramatically shortens the feedback loop from "idea" to "working prototype that business stakeholders can actually test." We've now deployed Dify in production for three enterprise clients across different verticals (financial services, e-commerce, and healthcare logistics). Here's what we learned about the multi-tenancy gap — and a proposal for bridging it. The Multi-Tenancy Reality Enterprise deployments are almost never single-tenant in the way most open-source tools assume. Even when a single organization deploys Dify, they typically need: Dimension Requirement Department isolation Finance and Customer Support use the same Dify instance but must not see each other's datasets, apps, or API keys. Role-based access Not just admin vs. user — but per-workspace roles (dataset editor, app viewer, prompt reviewer, deployment operator). Usage metering Each department needs separate cost tracking (token consumption, vector storage, API calls) for internal chargeback. Custom branding White-labeling per workspace in the chat UI. Currently, Dify's workspace model provides some separation, but it's primarily collaborative — members within a workspace see most shared resources. True data isolation, granular RBAC, and per-workspace usage metering require significant customization. A Pragmatic Proposal Rather than building a full multi-tenant SaaS layer (which may not align with Dify's product direction), we suggest an extension-point approach: Pluggable Authentication Backend — Allow organizations to wire in their own SSO/OIDC provider per workspace, with group-to-role mapping from the upstream IdP (Azure AD, Okta). This is the single highest-impact feature for enterprise adoption. Isolation Hooks — Expose middleware hooks at key boundaries (dataset queries, app execution, API key validation) where custom isolation logic can be injected. A simple Python plugin interface would let teams implement per-tenant data filtering without forking Dify. Metered Usage Exporter — A built-in Prometheus endpoint (or webhook sink) that emits per-workspace, per-user usage metrics. Teams can then build their own dashboards and billing integrations externally. The Good News Dify's architecture is clean enough that these extensions are feasible without a major rewrite. We've implemented a proof-of-concept using FastAPI middleware that wraps Dify's public API — it intercepts workspace context from JWT claims and filters dataset access accordingly. Initial results are promising, but a native plugin system would be far more maintainable. Has the community explored these patterns? We'd be happy to share our middleware implementation if others are facing the same multi-tenancy requirements.

originalLocation.context: Hi @l585826! I'm Dosu and I'm helping the Dify team. That usage is fine. Dify's license is a modified Apache 2.0, and the restriction it adds targets multi-tenant deployment, not how many end users call an app's API [1]. A "tenant" here maps to a Dify workspace. One workspace serving many end users who all hit the same app is standard single-tenant usage, and the license explicitly permits it commercially, including "as a backend service for other applications" [1]. What requires a written agreement from Dify is running Dify's source code to host multiple separate tenants — isolated customer workspaces and data — yourself [2]. A maintainer drew the same line in a related discussion, noting that multi-tenant deployment features are reserved for Dify's SaaS/Enterprise editions rather than the Community edition [3]. So many website visitors calling one chat app in one workspace via the API is allowed. Giving each of your own customers their own isolated workspace on the open-source code would cross into the restricted scenario and need a commercial license. Want me to dig into how end-user sessions are scoped within a single app via the API? To reply, just mention @dosu. Share context across your team and agents. Try Dosu.

returnedSources.snippet: Open Source 遵循 OSI（Open Source Initiative）认证的协议，如 Apache 2.0、MIT、GPL 等。这些协议赋予用户自由使用、修改、分发和商业化软件的权利，几乎没有限制。 Source-Available 则是一种混合模式：代码公开可见，但附加了限制性条款。这些条款通常精准地阻止某些商业用途，特别是那些可能与原作者形成竞争的场景。 ## Dify 协议的三大限制 让我们以 Dify 为例，分析其”修改版 Apache 2.0”协议的关键限制： ### 1. 多租户服务禁令 Dify 的协议明确规定： > “Unless explicitly authorized by Dify in writing, you may not use the Dify source code to operate a multi-tenant environment.” 这意味着： [...] 这意味着： ❌ 你不能使用 Dify 搭建一个 SaaS 平台，为多个客户提供独立的工作空间 ❌ 你不能成为 “Dify Cloud” 的竞争对手 ✅ 你只能为单一企业（单租户）部署 Dify 影响分析： 这条限制直接扼杀了 Dify 在云服务市场的潜在竞争对手。如果你是一家云服务提供商，想基于 Dify 为客户提供 AI 应用平台服务，你必须购买商业授权。这本质上是一种”引流”策略——通过开源获取用户和贡献，但将商业化路径牢牢控制在官方手中。 ### 2. LOGO 与品牌限制 > “In the process of using Dify’s frontend, you may not remove or modify the LOGO or copyright information.” 这意味着： ❌ 你不能进行白牌化（White-labeling） ❌ 你不能为客户提供完全定制的品牌体验 ✅ Dify 的品牌会随着软件的部署而传播 [...] ## 案例：从限制到自由 让我们通过一个真实场景，对比两种协议模式的差异： 场景： 你是一家系统集成商，想为多个医疗机构客户提供一个统一的 AI 知识库平台，每个医疗机构有独立的数据空间和品牌界面。 ### 方案A：使用 Dify（修改版 Apache 2.0） 协议限制： ❌ 多租户架构违反协议第 1.a 条（禁止多租户服务） ❌ 每个客户界面上必须显示 Dify LOGO（协议第 1.b 条） ❌ 需要联系官方购买商业授权 ❌ 授权费用不透明，可能随业务增长而增加 实际后果： 💰 初始授权费用 + 持续授权费用 🔒 技术决策受制于供应商 📉 客户对界面品牌不满意 ⚠️ 协议可能被单方面修改，增加未来风险 ### 方案B：使用 ApeRAG（标准 Apache 2.0） 协议自由： ✅ 天然支持多租户架构，每个医疗机构独立 workspace ✅ 完全自由定制品牌界面，无 LOGO 限制 ✅ 无需任何商业授权，零额外成本 ✅ 协议永久有效，不会被单方面修改 技术优势：
